correctness.rationale: For each integer m>=4, any positive budget and two-class price q>0, the grounded weighted Laplacian depends injectively on individual weights. Strict logdet concavity makes the maximizer unique, and rotation invariance forces constant weights per edge orbit. Its Fourier eigenproduct gives m*a^(2m-1)*(T_m(1+b/a)+1). The saturation parameter t=b/a gives endpoint slope (m*m-(2m-1)*q)/2, hence matching deletion iff q>=m*m/(2m-1); strict concavity gives one positive stationary point otherwise and handles equality. Compactness, connectedness, and the t=infinity degenerate limit justify global existence. The fixed-price positive root and critical q/m double-scaling emerge by boundedness plus derivative brackets. The local checker replay passed 815 exact/numerical assertions, which cannot certify infinitely many cases.

originality.rationale: The new statement is the global independently variable 2m-edge-plus-m-matching price-constrained D-optimal allocation for all m>=4, with the exact growing support threshold and two distinct asymptotic price regimes. The m=2 complete-graph and m=3 complete-bipartite cases are excluded as already covered. Primary literature gives general extremal metric equations or combinatorial edge selection, and the known Möbius-ladder sequence gives only the unweighted enumerator. Comparison does not support direct implication of the new closed-form optimization by the inspected prior theorems. Residual unlocated specialist overlap is acknowledged.

value.rationale: The exact financially meaningful edge-class screening price grows as m^2/(2m-1)~m/2 rather than staying fixed. The all-parameter optimizer includes strict uniqueness under individual, not assumed symmetric, allocations. Fixed-price positive rung usage contrasts with the nontrivial m^(-2) crossover at linearly scaling prices, governed by tanh(s/2)/s=alpha. The object is a canonical Möbius ladder; this nontrivial threshold and singular boundary layer are useful to weighted tree-optimal network investment and not an arbitrary finite case.
